FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 1
Sources of Hindu Law
Short Revision Note

Ancient sources include Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, and custom. Modern sources include legislation, judicial precedent, and justice, equity and good conscience. In a problem under a codified Act, begin with the Act and ask whether it expressly saves the claimed custom.
Detailed Study Note

Shruti refers to the revealed tradition, principally the Vedas. Smriti includes remembered traditions and texts such as those attributed to Manu and Yajnavalkya. Commentaries interpret particular texts and digests organise rules from multiple authorities. Mitakshara and Dayabhaga illustrate the development of distinct schools. Historical texts explain the origin of rules. Their present force depends on the applicable modern law.

Custom may be local, tribal, community, group or family based. Section 3(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) requires long, continuous and uniform observance giving the rule force of law, certainty, and compatibility with reasonableness and public policy. A family custom must also remain undiscontinued. The party invoking a disputed custom ordinarily pleads and proves it. Thakur Gokal Chand v Parvin Kumari, AIR 1952 SC 231, is a leading illustration of the evidentiary requirement.

Legislation now governs many areas of Hindu personal law. HMA section 4 displaces prior texts, rules and customs on matters for which the Act makes provision, subject to express savings. Binding precedent interprets legislation and develops doctrine. Justice, equity and good conscience has a residual role where applicable legal rules leave a gap.

Hypothetical illustration. A family claims that an ancestral practice permits marriage within prohibited degrees. Identify the statutory provision saving a qualifying custom, then ask what evidence proves the practice and its applicability to the parties.
Exam Practice
3 marks. What are Shruti and Smriti?
11 marks. Discuss the ancient and modern sources of Hindu law and the continuing role of custom.
Answer plan. Classify the sources, explain their role, then apply HMA sections 3(a) and 4 and cite Gokal Chand.
Self-test. Does an occasional family practice establish a binding custom?
Answer. Long, uniform observance and the other statutory requirements must be proved.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 2
Hindu Marriage Application Conditions Ceremonies and Registration
Short Revision Note

HMA section 2 governs application, section 5 conditions, section 7 customary ceremonies, and section 8 registration. Solemnisation and registration perform different functions. The legal consequence of violating a condition depends on the particular clause and statute.
Detailed Study Note

Section 2 covers Hindus in its statutory sense, including Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, and specified other persons. Members of Scheduled Tribes are excluded by section 2(2) unless the Central Government directs otherwise by notification. Apply the precise statutory categories in a problem.

Section 5 requires no living spouse, the prescribed mental capacity, minimum ages of 21 for the bridegroom and 18 for the bride, and compliance with prohibitions on prohibited degrees and sapinda relationships unless a governing custom permits the union. Sapinda limits extend to the third generation through the mother and fifth through the father, counting the person as the first generation. Section 11 applies only to section 5(i), (iv) and (v). Consider the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 separately for an underage marriage, including its ordinary voidability rule and specified void marriages.

Section 7 permits the customary rites of either party. If the rites include saptapadi, the marriage becomes complete on the seventh step. Section 8 facilitates proof through registration. In Dolly Rani v Manish Kumar Chanchal, 2024 INSC 355, the Supreme Court explained that a certificate cannot create a Hindu marriage where the requisite ceremonies were never performed. Non-registration itself does not affect validity under section 8(5).
Hypothetical illustration. A couple obtains a Hindu marriage certificate without any applicable customary ceremonies. Apply sections 7 and 8 and distinguish proof from solemnisation.
Dolly Rani v Manish Kumar Chanchal  |  Judgment text
Exam Practice
3 marks. What is a sapinda relationship?
11 marks. Explain HMA application and the conditions, ceremonies and registration of Hindu marriage.
Answer plan. Start with section 2, list section 5 conditions, explain section 7 and section 8, cite Dolly Rani and identify consequences.
Self-test. When is a marriage complete if the applicable rites include saptapadi?
Answer. On the seventh step.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 3
Restitution and Judicial Separation under Hindu Law
Short Revision Note

Under HMA section 9, a spouse may seek restitution if the other has withdrawn from their society without reasonable excuse. Section 10 judicial separation suspends the obligation to cohabit while the marital status continues.
Detailed Study Note

For restitution, establish a subsisting marriage and withdrawal from the other spouse’s society. The court must be satisfied as to the truth of the petition and absence of a legal ground to refuse relief. The explanation places the burden of proving reasonable excuse on the spouse who withdrew once that question arises. Cruelty or safety concerns can be relevant on the facts.

In Saroj Rani v Sudarshan Kumar Chadha, (1984) 4 SCC 90, the Supreme Court upheld section 9. A decree is not implemented through physical compulsion to cohabit. Distinguish execution under the procedural law from the separate divorce ground under section 13(1A)(ii) for no restitution for at least one year after the decree.

Under section 10, either spouse may rely on applicable section 13(1) grounds and the wife may also rely on section 13(2) grounds. Cohabitation is no longer obligatory once the decree is made. The court may rescind it if just and reasonable. No resumption of cohabitation for at least one year after the decree can support divorce under section 13(1A)(i).

Hypothetical illustration. A spouse living separately alleges sustained cruelty. Examine reasonable excuse in a restitution petition and ask independently whether the evidence establishes judicial separation.
Exam Practice
3 marks. State the effect of a judicial separation decree.
11 marks. Compare restitution and judicial separation under the HMA.
Answer plan. State sections 9 and 10, compare ingredients and effects, discuss Saroj Rani and link each decree to section 13(1A).
Self-test. Does judicial separation dissolve the marriage?
Answer. The marriage continues.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 4
Void and Voidable Hindu Marriages
Short Revision Note

Section 11 covers bigamy, prohibited degrees and sapinda relationships, subject to the custom exceptions in section 5. Section 12 covers marriages that remain valid unless annulled by decree. A petition for nullity is distinct from divorce.
Detailed Study Note

A marriage violating section 5(i), (iv) or (v) is void under section 11. Either party may seek a decree declaring nullity. The mental-capacity condition in section 5(ii) is addressed through section 12. Underage marriage requires separate attention to section 18 HMA and the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006.

Section 12(1) grounds are non-consummation owing to the respondent’s impotence, contravention of section 5(ii), consent obtained by force or fraud about the nature of the ceremony or a material fact or circumstance concerning the respondent, and the respondent’s pregnancy by another person at marriage.

For force or fraud, section 12(2) bars relief if more than one year has passed since force ceased or fraud was discovered, or if the petitioner thereafter lived with the other spouse with full consent. For pregnancy by another, the petitioner must have been ignorant at marriage, filed within the prescribed period, and not had consensual marital intercourse after discovering the ground. Apply section 16 separately for children.

Hypothetical illustration. A spouse discovers that the other had a living spouse when the marriage was solemnised. Apply sections 5(i) and 11, proving the subsisting earlier marriage and the facts of the later ceremony.
Exam Practice
3 marks. State the three grounds of voidness under section 11.
11 marks. Distinguish void and voidable Hindu marriages and explain the grounds and bars to annulment.
Answer plan. Compare legal status, list each statutory ground, explain section 12(2) and refer to section 16.
Self-test. Does age alone make a marriage void under section 11 HMA?
Answer. Section 11 does not list age. The child marriage legislation must also be considered.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 5
Divorce by Contest Consent and Custom under Hindu Law
Short Revision Note
HMA section 13 governs contested divorce, section 13B mutual consent and section 29(2) saved customary dissolution. For each route identify the ground, evidence and procedural conditions.
Detailed Study Note

Section 13(1) includes adultery, cruelty, desertion for at least two years immediately before presentation, conversion, prescribed mental disorder, communicable venereal disease, renunciation and being unheard of as alive for seven years. Leprosy was removed as a ground in 2019. Section 13(1A) addresses non-resumption after judicial separation or non-restitution after a restitution decree. Section 13(2) gives the wife special grounds, including specified sexual offences by the husband, qualifying maintenance orders followed by non-cohabitation, and repudiation of a marriage solemnised before she was 15 within the statutory age window. The historic pre-Act polygamy ground has distinct conditions.

Section 13B requires a joint petition after living separately for at least one year, inability to live together and mutual agreement to dissolve. The second motion is ordinarily between six and eighteen months from presentation, with consent continuing until decree. In Amardeep Singh v Harveen Kaur, (2017) 8 SCC 746, the Supreme Court held the six-month interval directory and waivable in suitable cases. Sureshta Devi v Om Prakash, (1991) 2 SCC 25, explains continuing consent.

Customary divorce requires proof of a qualifying applicable custom and compliance with its conditions. A private deed alone does not create the power to dissolve. Shilpa Sailesh v Varun Sreenivasan, 2023 INSC 468, concerns the Supreme Court’s distinct Article 142 power in cases of irretrievable breakdown. Ordinary courts apply the statutory grounds.

Hypothetical illustration. Spouses living separately for over a year agree on alimony and custody. Apply section 13B and distinguish statutory eligibility, continuing consent and possible waiver of the second-motion interval.
Exam Practice
3 marks. What does section 29(2) preserve?
11 marks. Explain contested, mutual-consent and customary divorce under the HMA.
Answer plan. Group section 13 grounds, set out section 13B and the waiver case, and distinguish proof of custom.
Self-test. Does waiver of the six-month interval dispense with continuing consent?
Answer. Both spouses’ consent must subsist until decree.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 6
Legitimacy of Children
Short Revision Note

HMA section 16 protects children of void marriages and qualifying children of voidable marriages annulled by decree. The protection does not validate the marriage. Property rights under section 16(3) concern property of the parents.
Detailed Study Note

Section 16(1) deems the child of a marriage void under section 11 legitimate if the child would have been legitimate had the marriage been valid. This applies regardless of whether a nullity decree was granted. Section 16(2) protects a child begotten or conceived before the decree annulling a voidable marriage where the child would otherwise have been legitimate.

In Revanasiddappa v Mallikarjun, 2023 INSC 783, the Supreme Court explained that a child protected by section 16 can succeed to a parent’s property, including the deceased parent’s ascertained share in joint family property under the applicable succession rules. The child does not acquire an independent coparcenary birthright by virtue of section 16 or a claim to the property of a person other than the parents.

Exam sequence. Identify the kind of marriage, identify the relevant subsection, state whether a decree and timing matter, then identify whose property is in issue. In an SMA problem its corresponding rule is section 26, which should be analysed on its own wording.

Hypothetical illustration. A father dies leaving an ascertainable interest in joint family property. Separate the father’s share, which may pass by succession, from a claim by the child to an independent share by birth.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Does section 16 legitimise the marriage itself?
11 marks. Discuss legitimacy and property rights under section 16 with Revanasiddappa.
Answer plan. Distinguish subsections (1) and (2), explain the parental-property limitation and illustrate the joint family issue.
Self-test. Does section 16 create an independent coparcenary right by birth?
Answer. No.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 7
Jurisdiction and Bars to Matrimonial Relief
Short Revision Note

Section 19 determines the territorial forum. Section 14 usually bars a divorce petition within the first year of marriage. Section 23 sets out conditions for granting relief. Check the competent forum and the statutory ground separately.
Detailed Study Note

Section 19 connects jurisdiction to solemnisation, respondent’s residence, the parties’ last joint residence, or the wife’s residence where she is petitioner. The petitioner’s residence also applies under the stated conditions when the respondent is outside the territories to which the Act extends or has not been heard of as alive for seven years. Where a Family Court has jurisdiction, read sections 7–8 of the Family Courts Act, 1984.

Section 14 permits early presentation with leave in exceptional hardship to the petitioner or exceptional depravity by the respondent. The section requires attention to children’s interests and reconciliation prospects. Section 15 governs when remarriage is lawful after divorce with reference to appeal rights, time and dismissal.

Section 23 requires proof of the ground and checks issues including taking advantage of one’s own wrong where applicable, condonation, connivance, collusion, improper delay and free mutual consent. Courts attempt reconciliation where possible and consistent with the circumstances and statutory exceptions. Dharmendra Kumar v Usha Kumar, (1977) 4 SCC 12, illustrates that mere disinclination to resume marital life is not necessarily a wrong sufficient to bar relief.

Hypothetical illustration. A wife moves to another district and files there. Determine her residence on presentation under section 19. Independently check whether the petition meets section 14 and whether section 23 bars relief.
Exam Practice
3 marks. List three territorial connections under section 19.
11 marks. Explain jurisdiction and bars to relief under the HMA.
Answer plan. Identify the proper court and territorial facts, explain the one-year rule and exceptions, then discuss section 23.
Self-test. What can justify leave to file divorce within the first year?
Answer. Exceptional hardship to the petitioner or exceptional depravity by the respondent.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT I  /  TOPIC 8
Interim Maintenance and Permanent Alimony
Short Revision Note

HMA section 24 deals with litigation expenses and support during proceedings. Section 25 concerns permanent alimony on passing a decree or subsequently. Either spouse may apply under the HMA. Read overlapping remedies separately and account for earlier awards.
Detailed Study Note

Section 24 looks to whether the applicant has independent income sufficient for support and necessary expenses of proceedings. The court considers both parties’ incomes and can order a reasonable monthly amount and litigation expenses. The Act sets a disposal target, as far as possible, of 60 days from service of notice.

Under section 25 the court can award a gross sum or periodical payments, for a term not exceeding the applicant’s life, considering income and property, conduct and other circumstances. The court may secure payment by a charge on immovable property and vary, modify or rescind the order on the statutory grounds. Interim maintenance and permanent alimony address different stages and purposes.

Rajnesh v Neha, (2021) 2 SCC 324, provides guidance on financial disclosure, overlapping proceedings, adjustment and ordinarily awarding maintenance from the application date. Compare HMA relief with independent statutory claims, including section 18 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, and section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (the successor to section 125 CrPC), where applicable.

Hypothetical illustration. A spouse earns a small amount insufficient for basic support and litigation. Evaluate sufficiency under section 24 and consider any existing award before calculating relief.
Exam Practice
3 marks. What does maintenance pendente lite mean?
11 marks. Distinguish sections 24 and 25 and explain the criteria for granting relief.
Answer plan. Compare timing, eligibility and forms of relief, then address disclosures, overlapping orders and variation.
Self-test. Can a husband apply under HMA section 24?
Answer. Yes. Either spouse may apply if the statutory requirements are met.
Unit I Revision Checklist
Recall. Sources and custom • Application and solemnisation • Sections 9–13B on relief • Legitimacy and jurisdiction • Sections 24–25 on maintenance.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 1
Special Marriage Conditions Solemnisation and Registration
Short Revision Note

The Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA) provides a civil marriage route. Sections 4–14 govern solemnisation. Sections 15–18 provide for registering certain marriages celebrated in another form. The two routes have different conditions.
Detailed Study Note

Section 4 requires neither party to have a living spouse, compliance with prescribed mental capacity, completion of 21 years by the male and 18 by the female, and compliance with prohibited-degree rules, subject to the statutory custom exception. The Act can be used by couples of different religions and does not require conversion.

Under sections 5–8, give written notice to the Marriage Officer of a district in which at least one party has resided for at least thirty days immediately before notice. The statute provides for publication, objections within thirty days on section 4 grounds and inquiry. State the statutory process when answering a question. Under sections 11–13 the parties and three witnesses sign a declaration, the parties make the required words of acceptance before the Officer and witnesses, and the certificate is entered. Section 14 ordinarily requires fresh notice if solemnisation does not occur within three calendar months, subject to its appeal-related rule.

Section 15 concerns registration of an existing ceremony. Its conditions include living together as spouses since the ceremony, no more than one living spouse each, prescribed capacity, completion of age 21 by both at registration, prohibited-degree rules with the statutory proviso, and district residence by the parties for the required period. Sections 16–18 address the procedure, appeal and legal effect of entry.

Hypothetical illustration. A woman aged 19 and a man aged 23 ask about an SMA civil ceremony. The section 4 age rule may be met. If they instead seek registration of an earlier ceremony under section 15, both must be 21 at registration.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Distinguish the age conditions in sections 4 and 15.
11 marks. Explain conditions, solemnisation and registration under the SMA.
Answer plan. Compare the routes, set out residence and notice, explain declarations and certificate and distinguish their effects.
Self-test. How many witnesses attend solemnisation under section 12?
Answer. Three.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 2
Restitution and Judicial Separation under the Special Marriage Act
Short Revision Note

SMA section 22 addresses withdrawal from a spouse’s society without reasonable excuse. Section 23 permits judicial separation on applicable divorce grounds or failure to comply with a restitution decree.
Detailed Study Note

Section 22 allows the aggrieved spouse to petition the district court where the other spouse has withdrawn without reasonable excuse. Establish a valid subsisting marriage and withdrawal. The court must be satisfied that the statements are true and that no legal ground bars relief. The statutory explanation places the burden of proving reasonable excuse on the withdrawing spouse when the question arises.

Under section 23 either spouse can seek judicial separation on grounds specified in section 27(1), and the wife can also rely on applicable grounds under section 27(1A). Failure to comply with a restitution decree furnishes a separate ground under section 23. A judicial separation decree ends the obligation to cohabit without dissolving the marriage. The court may rescind the decree where just and reasonable.

Section 27(2) separately allows either party to seek divorce following at least one year without resumption of cohabitation after judicial separation, or without restitution after a restitution decree. A new divorce proceeding and decree are required. Check section 34 for the court’s conditions for relief.

Hypothetical illustration. A spouse has a judicial separation decree, and the parties have not resumed cohabitation for more than a year. Identify their existing status and the separate divorce ground under section 27(2).
Exam Practice
3 marks. What is the effect of an SMA judicial separation decree?
11 marks. Compare sections 22 and 23 and explain their relevance to divorce under section 27(2).
Answer plan. State the ingredients, compare grounds and effects, then explain the one-year divorce grounds.
Self-test. Does a restitution decree itself terminate a marriage?
Answer. No.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 3
Void and Voidable Marriages under the Special Marriage Act
Short Revision Note

SMA section 24 states grounds of voidness and section 25 grounds for annulment of a voidable marriage. Its list differs from the HMA. Identify the statutory route before deciding whether a marriage is void or voidable.
Detailed Study Note

Under section 24(1), a marriage solemnised under the Act is void if a condition in section 4(a)–(d) was not fulfilled, or if the respondent was impotent at marriage and at institution of the suit. Either party may petition for a decree of nullity. Section 24(2) gives a separate route to declare certain Chapter III registrations of no effect on stated section 15 grounds.

Section 25 covers non-consummation owing to the respondent’s wilful refusal, pregnancy by another person at marriage, and consent obtained through coercion or fraud as defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872. For pregnancy, check ignorance at marriage, timely proceedings and absence of consensual marital intercourse after discovery. For coercion or fraud, check the one-year limit from cessation or discovery and whether the petitioner freely lived with the spouse thereafter.

The core exam distinction is that impotence at both relevant times appears under section 24, whereas wilful refusal to consummate appears under section 25. Read section 26 separately for legitimacy and parental-property limits.

Hypothetical illustration. A spouse alleges that the respondent deliberately refused to consummate the marriage. Under the SMA, analyse the alleged conduct under section 25(i) and distinguish proof of impotence under section 24.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Identify two grounds under section 25.
11 marks. Distinguish void and voidable SMA marriages with particular reference to impotence and wilful refusal.
Answer plan. Explain section 24 and cross-reference section 4, list section 25 grounds and bars, and mention section 26.
Self-test. Which provision covers wilful refusal to consummate?
Answer. Section 25(i).
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 4
Divorce and Mutual Consent under the Special Marriage Act
Short Revision Note

Section 27 contains contested divorce grounds. Section 28 governs divorce by mutual consent. Section 29 usually bars a divorce petition within one year of the marriage certificate being entered, subject to leave on specified grounds.
Detailed Study Note

Section 27(1) includes adultery, desertion for at least two years, a sentence of imprisonment for seven years or more in the statutory terms, cruelty, prescribed mental disorder, communicable venereal disease and being unheard of as alive for seven years. Leprosy was removed in 2019. The wife’s special grounds in section 27(1A) include specified sexual offences by the husband and qualifying maintenance orders followed by at least one year without resumed cohabitation. Section 27(2) covers the specified failure to resume cohabitation or obtain restitution after decree.

Under section 28, both parties jointly petition after living separately for at least one year, being unable to live together and agreeing to dissolve. Their second motion is ordinarily within six to eighteen months after presentation if the petition is not withdrawn. The court hears the parties, makes the necessary inquiry and grants a decree when statutory requirements are satisfied. Identify any waiver authority applicable to the forum before assuming that an HMA ruling governs the SMA motion.

Jurisdiction is addressed in section 31 and conditions for relief in section 34. For an early contested petition under section 29, examine exceptional hardship to the petitioner or exceptional depravity by the respondent, plus the statutory considerations governing leave.
Hypothetical illustration. A couple has lived separately for thirteen months and wants a consent decree. Verify the marriage certificate, continuing consent and the section 28 motion requirements.
Exam Practice
3 marks. State the basic conditions for a joint petition under section 28.
11 marks. Explain divorce by contest and by mutual consent under the SMA.
Answer plan. Group the section 27 grounds, state timing and conditions under sections 28–29 and distinguish the two routes.
Self-test. Does living apart for one year by itself entitle the parties to a section 28 decree?
Answer. The parties must also meet the other statutory conditions and obtain a decree.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 5
Muslim Marriage and Dower
Short Revision Note

Muslim marriage or nikah is commonly explained as a civil contract with legal and social incidents. Review capacity, consent, offer and acceptance, witnesses where required, impediments and dower. Sahih means valid, batil void, and fasid irregular in the schools recognising the distinction.
Detailed Study Note

Offer and acceptance generally take place at the same meeting, directly or through authorised representatives. Examine capacity and consent alongside applicable legislation including the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. Classical personal-law statements about puberty should be distinguished from statutory child marriage rules. Witness and classification rules can vary between schools.

Absolute impediments include specified relationships of blood, affinity and fosterage. The consequences of other impediments, such as absence of required witnesses or marrying a fifth wife, can depend on the applicable school. Under Sunni doctrine an irregular union may have certain effects after consummation, including dower and legitimacy of children in applicable circumstances. Avoid assuming that all schools apply the fasid category identically. Chand Patel v Bismillah Begum, (2008) 4 SCC 774, illustrates a temporary impediment involving unlawful conjunction in Sunni law.

Dower or mahr is an obligation owed by the husband to the wife as an incident of marriage. It may be specified or proper dower, and prompt or deferred. Failure to fix the amount does not by itself invalidate the marriage. Prompt dower is generally payable on demand and deferred dower on the stipulated event. In Abdul Kadir v Salima (1886) ILR 8 All 149, the Full Bench discussed marriage, unpaid dower and restitution. Dower payable to the wife is distinct from prohibited dowry.

Hypothetical illustration. The parties agree no initial amount of mahr. Determine whether proper dower is due and examine any evidence relevant to its assessment before concluding that nothing is owed.
Exam Practice
3 marks. Distinguish prompt and deferred dower.
11 marks. Distinguish sahih, batil and fasid marriage and explain the legal incidents of dower.
Answer plan. Explain formation and impediments, discuss school-specific classification and consequences, then define and classify dower.
Self-test. Does failure to specify mahr necessarily invalidate nikah?
Answer. No. Proper dower may be payable.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 6
Divorce under Muslim Law
Short Revision Note

Distinguish classical forms of dissolution from statutory and judicial controls. Talaq, delegated talaq, khula and mubaraat are distinct concepts. Instant and irrevocable talaq covered by the 2019 Act is void and illegal.
Detailed Study Note

Classical classifications include talaq-e-ahsan, commonly described as a single pronouncement followed by the prescribed waiting period, and talaq-e-hasan, involving successive pronouncements at prescribed intervals. Talaq-e-biddat historically referred to an instantaneous and irrevocable form. Talaq al-bain describes irrevocability in classical terminology. The meaning and consequences depend on the form and applicable law.

In Shamim Ara v State of U.P., (2002) 7 SCC 518, the Supreme Court held that a bare plea of an earlier talaq did not effect a divorce and discussed reasonable cause and prior reconciliation. Shayara Bano v Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 1, set aside instant triple talaq by majority. Sections 2(c), 3 and 4 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 address the covered instant and irrevocable pronouncement, its voidness and illegality, and punishment. Sections 5 and 6 concern subsistence allowance and custody.

Talaq-e-tafweez refers to delegated power agreed in an appropriate instrument, subject to its terms and applicable law. Khula is initiated by the wife and may entail return or adjustment of dower. Questions about consent and the legal effect of particular steps require attention to governing precedent. Mubaraat is mutual release. A wife may also seek a judicial decree under the 1939 Act. In Mohd Abdul Samad v State of Telangana, 2024 INSC 506, the Supreme Court confirmed that section 125 CrPC was available to a divorced Muslim woman alongside the statutory framework of the 1986 Act. For new proceedings consider BNSS section 144 and transition rules.

Hypothetical illustration. A husband sends an instant and irrevocable triple talaq message. Apply the statutory definition and sections 3–4. Consider any claim for subsistence allowance or custody separately.
Mohd Abdul Samad v State of Telangana  |  Supreme Court judgment
Exam Practice
3 marks. What is talaq-e-tafweez?
11 marks. Explain the modes of Muslim divorce, with the effect of Shamim Ara, Shayara Bano and the 2019 Act.
Answer plan. Classify modes, distinguish instant talaq, explain statutory consequences and identify the judicial route.
Self-test. Does a pronouncement covered by section 3 of the 2019 Act dissolve the marriage?
Answer. It is void and illegal.
FAMILY LAW I  /  UNIT II  /  TOPIC 7
Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939
Short Revision Note

Section 2 permits a wife married under Muslim law to seek a judicial decree on one or more specified grounds. Learn the time periods, proof requirements and special provisos. Section 5 preserves rights to dower.
Detailed Study Note

Section 2 grounds include the husband’s whereabouts being unknown for four years, failure to provide maintenance for two years, sentence of imprisonment for seven years or more, failure without reasonable cause to perform marital obligations for three years, impotence at marriage continuing thereafter, insanity for two years or virulent venereal disease, and specified repudiation of a marriage arranged before age fifteen. For repudiation it must occur before age eighteen and the marriage must not have been consummated. Leprosy was removed as a ground in 2019.

Cruelty includes habitual assault or conduct making life miserable, association with women of ill repute or leading an infamous life, attempting to force an immoral life, interference with the wife’s property rights, obstruction of religious practice, and inequitable treatment among wives where applicable. Section 2(ix) saves other grounds recognised under Muslim law.

Procedure. A decree based on the husband’s absence takes effect after six months and may be set aside on the statutory showing. Section 3 governs notice to persons who would be his heirs in that case, with additional notice requirements. An imprisonment sentence must be final. On the husband’s application on the impotence ground, the court must allow the statutory opportunity to show cessation. Under section 4, renunciation of Islam or conversion by a married Muslim woman does not by itself dissolve the marriage, subject to the section’s stated exception. Section 5 preserves dower rights.

Hypothetical illustration. A wife says that her husband has been missing for four years. Identify section 2(i), gather proof of absence, apply section 3 notice and explain the delayed operation of the decree.
Exam Practice
3 marks. State two grounds with their time periods.
11 marks. Discuss the grounds and procedure for a decree under the 1939 Act.
Answer plan. Group the grounds, give exact periods, explain special notice and provisos and finish with sections 4–5.
Self-test. Does the decree automatically extinguish dower rights?
Answer. Section 5 preserves the rights to dower she may have under Muslim law.
Unit II Revision Checklist
Recall. SMA solemnisation and registration • Sections 22–28 on relief • Muslim marriage and dower • Forms of divorce and the 1939 and 2019 Acts.
